Dear Representative Anderson,
I am writing as a Birth to Three Developmental Therapist and Team Manager at @ Lumibility, who works directly with children and families served through Connecticut’s Birth to Three program. I am deeply concerned that without immediate and sustained funding, the Birth to Three system is at serious risk of collapse.

Birth to Three is a federally mandated early intervention program under IDEA Part C. Eligible children are legally entitled to services, and providers cannot create waitlists or pause enrollment when funding falls short. Demand continues to grow, yet reimbursement does not cover the true cost of delivering services. This funding gap is placing unsustainable pressure on the workforce. Birth to Three is entirely staff driven. When therapists leave, the impact is immediate: caseloads are redistributed, remaining staff are stretched beyond capacity, burnout increases, and additional staff losses become more likely. Each vacancy puts further strain on an already fragile system.

Connecticut is already seeing the consequences. According to the state’s own Birth to Three Rate Study, reimbursement rates do not cover the full cost of services, and the cost data used is already several years old. As a result, overall service intensity statewide has dropped significantly compared to prior years, even as demand has increased. Providers are being forced to absorb losses simply to meet federally required service obligations.
If this system continues to weaken, the outcome is predictable:
•	Children will miss critical early intervention during the most important period of brain development
•	Families will experience increased stress and instability
•	Children will require more intensive and costly special education services later
•	Childcare providers will struggle to meet children’s needs, increasing the risk of expulsion
•	Parents may be forced to reduce work hours or leave the workforce altogether

This is not a cost saving scenario. Failure to invest now simply shifts significantly higher costs to school districts, families, and the broader economy later.

What we are asking you to do

To prevent system failure and stabilize Connecticut’s federally mandated Birth to Three program, I respectfully urge you to support the following investments, spread across the next two fiscal years:
1.	Reinstate the statutory General Administrative Payment (GAP) language that provides $200 per eligible child, which was intended to stabilize the Birth to Three system until sustainable reimbursement rates were achieved — a point we have not yet reached.
2.	Restore the $1 million reduction to GAP funding included in the proposed budget, which further weakens an already strained system.
3.	Add $17.7 million to the DSS Birth to Three budget across two years, in alignment with the state sanctioned cost study, so providers can cover the true cost of delivering federally required services.
4.	Fund the Office of Early Childhood (OEC) Birth to Three budget at $23.3 million across two years, recognizing OEC’s critical role in administering and supporting the system.
5.	Ensure that these investments are not tied to the proposed expanded tiered reimbursement structure, which does not support workforce recruitment, retention, or program stability.
6.	Adopt legislative language requiring regular review and adjustment of Birth to Three rates, so funding keeps pace with inflation and does not continue to fall behind actual costs.

Without these actions, agencies will continue to lose staff like me, reduce their capacity to serve Connecticut's children, or agencies to conclude their contracts in the system entirely — and once that capacity is lost, it will be far more costly and difficult to rebuild.

Sincerely,
Julie Retier
Developmental Therapist/Kidsteps by Lumibility
Cromwell, Portland, Glastonbury, Middletown, Wethersfield, Rocky Hill

Testimony:

Written Testimony Opposing H.B. 5468
An Act Concerning the Provision of Equivalent Instruction

To the Honorable Members of the Education Committee,

My name is Reverend Michael A. Sypek. I am the pastor of Pilgrim Covenant Church in Granby, and I live in Granby, Connecticut. I write in opposition to H.B. 5468. The bill would formalize new reporting and review requirements for families providing “equivalent instruction.” 
I write not only as a citizen, but as a Christian, a parent, and a pastor. I am deeply concerned that this bill would move Connecticut away from respecting parents as the primary stewards of their children’s upbringing and toward a system of increased state oversight over families who are conscientiously seeking to educate their children outside the public-school system.
As written, H.B. 5468 would require families providing equivalent instruction to enter a more formal compliance system involving intent-to-educate forms, continuation forms, annual demonstrations of equivalent instruction, and multi-year retention of educational records. For families withdrawing a child from public school to begin equivalent instruction, the bill would also require a DCF-related review before that withdrawal could take effect. Whatever the stated intent of the bill, the practical effect is to place new burdens of paperwork, review, and uncertainty on homeschooling families who are already working hard to educate their children faithfully and responsibly. 

These are not small concerns. Many homeschooling families already make significant financial and personal sacrifices to provide for the education of their children, while also continuing to support the public-school system through their taxes. H.B. 5468 would add further costs in time, administration, and in some cases money, all for families who are not seeking to evade responsibility, but to fulfill it. The bill does include access to up to two public-school classes and extracurricular activities for children receiving equivalent instruction, but the overall direction is still one of added oversight and compliance. 

I am also concerned that this bill does not stand alone. It feels like one more turn of the ratchet in a state that already stripped away the religious vaccine exemption and has allowed public-school confusion over sex and gender to erode the sex-based protections Title IX was enacted to preserve. The result is not just legal confusion, but a broader degradation of morality, parental trust, and social order. Connecticut eliminated the religious exemption to school immunization requirements in 2021, and Title IX is the federal law that prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex in federally funded education programs. 

That is especially troubling in Connecticut, a state with proud religious traditions. Our constitution acknowledges the good providence of God, and it protects the free exercise of religion. These are not hollow words. They reflect a tradition in which liberty of conscience, religious duty, and family responsibility have long been treated as central to a free society.
As an American who values First Amendment freedoms, I believe we should be very cautious about policies that increasingly treat faithful parents less as responsible stewards and more as subjects of suspicion. The state certainly has a legitimate interest in the education and safety of children. But that interest should be exercised with restraint, humility, and respect for the prior responsibility of parents to direct the upbringing of their children.

While I believe proper protections for children are in the best interest of society—and certainly in the interest of Christian people—this bill can only be understood as an overcorrection to a problem limited in scope. It reflects a troubling drift toward the profoundly un-American notion that children belong to the state rather than to their parents, whom God has entrusted to be their primary protectors and educators. The state has a role, yes—but it is a secondary one, and it must never be allowed to eclipse the authority and responsibility God has given to the family.

Parents are not the enemy. Families who homeschool are not a problem to be managed simply because they have chosen a different path. In many cases, they are doing so out of deep conviction, sacrifice, and love for their children’s intellectual, moral, and spiritual formation.
One unintended consequence of this bill may be an exodus from Connecticut of the very families our communities can least afford to lose: Christian families, freedom-loving families, and other conscientious parents who have chosen to remain here despite the many burdens of living in this state and what many increasingly experience as hostility toward religious conviction and parental authority. Bills like this do not merely add regulation; they send a message about what kinds of families are welcome here. For families like mine, and for many of the families I minister to and share deep fellowship with, legislation of this kind makes staying in Connecticut more difficult to justify.

That would be a genuine loss not only for local churches, but for our towns, our state, and New England more broadly. Strong families build strong communities. Families of conviction are often the very ones serving their neighbors, strengthening churches, supporting civic life, and raising children to become responsible and faithful citizens. Connecticut should not be driving such families away.

I respectfully urge this Committee to reject H.B. 5468.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
Reverend Michael A. Sypek
Pilgrim Covenant Church
Granby, Connecticut

Dear Representative Anderson,

 

I am a Connecticut retired public school teacher, and a member of the Association of Retired Teachers of Connecticut (ARTC).

First, thank you for your service to the people of Connecticut. As retired teachers, we no longer have a union to negotiate retirement benefits on our behalf. We rely on the legislature to protect the pension and health benefits we earned through decades of service to our students and our state.

I am writing to ask for your support on two important issues affecting retired teachers:

 

1. Restore the One-Third Health Insurance Subsidy

Retired teachers pay most of our health insurance costs, even with contributions from our Health Insurance Account. The state’s long-promised one-third subsidy now applies only to the Advantage Plan’s premium and does not fully apply to the Medicare Supplement Plan’s premium. Neither of the two plans cover Medicare Part B or dental coverage costs.

Many retirees depend on Original Medicare with the Supplement plan to maintain stable access to providers and predictable coverage. We respectfully ask that the full one-third subsidy be restored to the Medicare Supplement Plan and that Original Medicare remain an affordable option for retirees who need it. 

 

2. Update the Teachers’ Retirement Board (TRB) Election Process

Following the expansion of retired-teacher representation on the TRB, unanimously supported by the legislature, ARTC is proposing a clearer, constituent-based election system: retired teacher representatives elected by retirees, and active teacher representatives elected by active teachers.

With the next TRB nominating process beginning in 2027, legislative action is needed this session to ensure a fair and transparent constituent-based election structure moving forward.

 

I respectfully ask that you not only support these proposals, but also speak with leadership on the Appropriations Committee about including these items in the legislature’s budget proposal this session.

 

These issues are deeply important to me and to all retired teachers. I hope you will advocate for us during budget negotiations.

 

Thank you for your time and consideration.

 

Sincerely,
Marianne Malliet
Granby, CT

HB 5222 is presented as a Department of Consumer Protection (DCP) clean-up bill, but Sections 1 and 2 shift a fundamental power in how Connecticut enforces CPA rules.

Today, the State Board of Accountancy is the entity with real authority over CPA discipline. DCP investigates, but the Board, made up of CPAs, is the expert body that decides whether standards have been violated and what discipline is appropriate.

Sections 1 and 2 of HB 5222 rewrite that structure by giving DCP the same enforcement tools as the Board and allowing DCP to use them on its own, “in either’s discretion.” DCP can conduct hearings, issue cease‑and‑desist orders, go to court, and impose civil penalties of up to $50,000 in CPA cases without any requirement to notify the Board, consult the Board, or follow the Board’s determinations.

That is not “sharing” authority – it is taking what has effectively been the Board’s authority and giving it to DCP. Over time, DCP can bring fewer and fewer matters to the Board until the Board becomes a bystander.

Why This is Dangerous

The Board of Accountancy was created because CPA regulation is highly technical and constantly changing. Its members are CPAs who understand audits, attest work, peer review, and professional ethics.
DCP does not employ practicing CPAs and has already made serious mistakes enforcing CPA rules – including blocking license renewals and threatening fines for lawful marketing because staff misunderstood basic peer review requirements.

Thank you for your continued work to represent the people of Connecticut, Representative Steve.  Please oppose SB146 and keep Connecticut a state where we act based on science-researched knowledge, common sense, and with the highest regard for life, including both for people and our natural world.
SB146 presents the killing of bears as a way to prevent bears from seeking food near people or farmers’ livestock.  Science and common sense show that killing bears will NOT stop remaining bears from seeking food in the same manner.  Instead, removing food attractants (securing trash, removing bird feeders), protecting livestock with electric fencing (which is highly effective with bears), and keeping dogs on leash — are the most effective ways to avoid problems with bears.  As well as continuing to educate regarding the above methods of reducing unwanted interactions with bears, our State could explore accessing low-cost bear-proof trash containers (especially to those in need of financial help) and help to farmers with the costs of electric fencing.  The above proven preventative measures will help people and bears safely coexist.
In addition, it is essential that Connecticut continue to make progress in creating connected Greenways throughout our state.  Such greenways should lead to the greenways of neighboring states and to coastal preserves.  Preserving greenways addresses both the climate crisis (CT nature draws down and safely stores vast quantities of CO2) and biodiversity crisis, among our highest priority of crises to address.  Greenways give bears and other wildlife the habitat they require to find food in nature and also keep them from unwanted interactions with people.  
SB146 does not address any problems effectively, perpetuates cruelty, and isn’t in keeping with Connecticut residents’ values.  DEEP's current policy already mandates killing orphaned bear cubs under 60 pounds – which is objectively cruel and an outdated, unimaginative way to deal with orphaned babies, especially of animals native to our area.  Bear killing and hunting will only create more suffering, more danger (including to the public and other non-target animals), and more violence.  We know these are not the answer to any problem.  Please oppose SB146.  
Sincerely, 
Ann Z.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to Senate Bill 146, An Act Concerning the Protection of Livestock from Certain Wildlife. While protecting agricultural interests is important, this bill significantly expands when and how wildlife — including bears — may be killed by broadening permit authority and loosening safeguards, and by expressly allowing individuals to use deadly physical force against bears if they believe livestock is being harmed. Under the bill’s proposed changes, permits could be issued for taking wildlife that threatens or has caused damage during the previous growing season, and the criteria for lethal force against bears would be widened beyond self-defense to include perceived livestock threat — a shift that risks prioritizing lethal outcomes over coexistence and will put Connecticut’s growing bear population in greater peril.  ￼

Connecticut has a strong tradition of valuing both its agricultural heritage and its wildlife. Rather than broad legal changes that make it easier to kill bears and other wildlife, we should be focusing on proven nonlethal strategies and coexistence measures that protect both farmers and ecosystems. Expanding lethal options undermines long-term wildlife management goals and could lead to unnecessary harm to bears that are otherwise not a threat to public safety. I urge you to oppose SB146 and support balanced, science-based approaches that protect livestock while preserving our natural heritage.

Dear Representative Kennedy,
Hello! My name is Jenna Bagdasarian and I am an MSW student at Southern Connecticut State University. I would first like to express my gratitude for your representation of Milford and for taking the time to hear from me today. I am reaching out to inform you of my support for HB 5166 to eliminate the Social Work Licensing Exam. I was hoping to submit a written testimony, but unfortunately was having some trouble navigating where to submit the testimony, so I thought I could write to you directly. 
I wish to inform you today of my personal and ethical concerns regarding the LMSW Licensure Exam. After completing my Bachelor's in Social Work at the University of New Hampshire, I moved on to the one-year Advanced Standing Program at Southern. I was unaware of the exam until this year, as the exam is making a return after several years of social workers being licensed without needing to take it. Not only does the sudden return of the exam add stress to us, already hard-working students, but the LMSW exam is not representative of the communities in which we serve and the ethical standards in which we practice. As Social Workers, we learn not to look solely at the problem a person comes to us with, but rather their experiences and environment, which led them to where they are, and their strengths that can empower them to work through difficult times. The LMSW exam is not about showing up for the people we work with; it is about the order in which to do it. However, meeting the needs of people requires being flexible, being able to pivot, and taking from multiple social work skills and resources. There is no one right answer in social work, so why is it expected of us to pick out "right" answers for 4 hours in order to work with the clients that we have been working with through our countless hours of internships and years of studying? Additionally, many of the questions on the exam are not representative of the communities in which we work, and only contribute to furthering unjust power dynamics and hierarchies between clients and social workers.
Pivoting to a more personal story. I have done three internships total in my time as a social work student. I have had the opportunity to learn from application through several years of hard work and dedication towards supporting others. I find so much passion in social work, and it saddens me to say that in preparation for this exam, I have lost some of the excitement that I previously had. This is because not only was finding out about the exam a shock, but then navigating receiving accommodations has become an additional barrier. I have ADHD, which I like to describe as being a tulip in a rose garden. Tulips and roses are both great flowers, with differing needs. Having to be my own advocate my entire life is one of the reasons I wanted to become a social worker. So, when I began the request process to recieve accomodations back in December, I thought that I would receive notice back by now. That has not happened. Then, once I do hear back, and if I can receive accommodations, the exam would then become 6 hours long. I would have to figure out where I am able to take the exam that meets the needs of my disability, and try to schedule the exam with dates already being booked up all the way until summer. It is limiting for me to even access the exam, let alone take it. It has become incredibly frustrating to graduate Summa Cum Laude from my BSW, have a 4.0 GPA in my MSW, work directly with clients unpaid for 3 years, and then have to take an exam that is not accessible or representative of the work that we do. So, I write to your to urge you to support this bill and talk to other representatives to get on board as well. Information is power, and I hope you found this information helpful. 
I greatly appreciate you taking the time to read my message, and I hope if possible, it could be shared with other representatives in the House. This issue impacts not only social workers but the people we work with, and I do not think one exam can represent all the hard work social workers put in every day to try to improve the lives of others. Thank you.

I am writing as a Connecticut constituent to request your support in establishing and resourcing a dedicated Defense Support of Civil Authorities (DSCA) aviation mission in Connecticut that leverages Connecticut Army National Guard rotary-wing assets for search-and-rescue (SAR), missing persons in wooded terrain, technical extraction/hoist operations, FLIR-enabled searches, and aerial firefighting with Bambi buckets.

DSCA exists specifically so National Guard capabilities can be used—when requested—to support civil authorities during domestic emergencies and other public safety incidents. It is a core component of the Guard’s mission set and designed precisely for situations where civilian resources are strained or lack specialized capability.

Connecticut currently does not maintain a consistently available, statewide aviation capability purpose-built for hoist rescue combined with FLIR search and multi-platform extraction, despite repeated incidents that demonstrate the need. A recent example is the rope rescue at Lantern Hill in North Stonington, where responders were faced with a complex cliff rescue requiring significant manpower, technical skill, and time. Similar incidents occur regularly across the state involving lost or injured hikers in remote wooded areas, including searches near the tri-state marker in Thompson and other rural regions.

While the Connecticut State Police Aviation Unit provides valuable service, its capacity is finite and not designed to serve as a full-time hoist rescue and aerial firefighting platform statewide. In contrast, the Connecticut Army National Guard aviation units operate UH-60M Black Hawks, HH-60M MEDEVAC aircraft, and CH-47 Chinooks—airframes inherently capable of:
	•	Forward Looking Infrared (FLIR) nighttime searches for missing persons
	•	Hoist and rescue basket extractions from cliffs, ravines, and heavily wooded terrain
	•	Multiple extrication platforms including hoist, landing zone operations, and external lift
	•	Aerial firefighting operations utilizing Bambi buckets

The Connecticut National Guard has already demonstrated the effectiveness of these capabilities. During the 2024 Hawthorne Brush Fire on Lamentation Mountain in Berlin, Guard aviation assets deployed Bambi buckets and reportedly dropped nearly a quarter-million gallons of water in support of local firefighting efforts. Guard aviation has also publicly documented joint aerial firefighting training utilizing UH-60M and CH-47 aircraft with Bambi bucket systems.

However, these missions are currently reactive and episodic—not structured under a formalized, standing DSCA aviation framework dedicated to search-and-rescue and wildfire response.

Other states have implemented successful models. The New Hampshire National Guard operates a well-established search-and-rescue partnership that regularly performs hoist rescues in mountainous and wooded terrain. In documented missions, hoist extractions were completed in minutes—where ground removal would have required hours. Connecticut should adopt a similar model tailored to our terrain, trail systems, and rural communities.

This need is particularly acute in:
	•	Northwest Connecticut’s elevated terrain and forest systems
	•	Eastern Connecticut’s large wooded tracts and limited access areas
	•	Rural zones where EMS transport times to definitive care are extended

In these settings, a Guard-supported DSCA aviation mission would:
	1.	Reduce time-to-location for missing persons using FLIR and coordinated air/ground search operations.
	2.	Reduce time-to-extrication when terrain prevents rapid ground evacuation.
	3.	Improve patient outcomes by shortening time to advanced medical care.
	4.	Increase rescuer safety by limiting prolonged, high-risk rope operations when hoist extraction is safer.
	5.	Provide rapid aerial firefighting capability during brush and wildland incidents threatening communities.

Connecticut possesses aviation assets with hoist, MEDEVAC, FLIR, and heavy-lift capabilities that are currently underutilized in a structured domestic response role. Establishing a formal DSCA aviation SAR and wildfire mission would enhance public safety without creating an entirely new system—simply by formalizing and resourcing what already exists.

I respectfully request your support in:
	•	Developing a formal DSCA aviation SAR and aerial firefighting concept of operations
	•	Funding and implementing recurring joint training between Guard aviation and state/local responders
	•	Establishing clear activation criteria and statewide integration
	•	Ensuring sustainable support so this capability is predictable and reliable

Connecticut residents recreate outdoors year-round. When emergencies occur in cold weather, rugged terrain, or remote areas, time is critical. We have the aircraft, personnel, and mission authority. What is needed now is structured implementation.

Thank you for your consideration and for your service to our state. I would welcome the opportunity to further discuss this proposal.

Respectfully,

Charles Weinsteiger

I am a resident of Oxford Connecticut and a registered Republican. I am active in my community through my leadership roles in our local youth organizations, though I do not hold any government positions.

I've seen several postings recently from Connecticut Republicans about a plan to improve affordability in Connecticut, clearly something we should all want to get behind. There is one aspect of the plan though that I disagree with and suggest that the party walk back from - "elimination" of the car tax. I'm generally a proponent of very small and limited government and hence believe that *all* taxes should be significantly reduced and/or eliminated, but the car tax (and other local property taxes) should be the last thing to address - and should not be within the purview of state level legislators.

Connecticut has a multitude of taxes that can be reduced or eliminated - income tax, gas tax (both retail and gross receipt), sales tax, prepared food tax, etc - let's face it, there is very little that Connecticut *doesn't* tax. Car and property taxes are not Connecticut state taxes though, they represent essentially the only means a municipality has of raising revenue independent of the state. This point is especially noteworthy given the unprecedented seizure of local control we saw from the administration this year related to zoning.

My understanding of this current proposal is that it will create an income tax credit that will essentially be a reimbursement by the state of taxes paid to their municipality. In doing so this will require "all" CT taxpayers to fund budgetary decisions of individual towns and cities. As a resident of fiscally responsible Oxford with a mill rate of 20.01 (tip of the hat to the Oxford Republicans) I will receive a credit for the taxes paid on my RAM 1500 to Oxford, but will be responsible to help reimburse a taxpayer with that very same vehicle in Bridgeport - where their decisions and voting history have led to a mill rate of 32.46. Why vote for fiscally responsible policies when someone else is going to foot the bill?

This is made worse given that the income tax credit is eliminated for those with only slightly more than modest incomes. One can look at an income of $100k for an individual and $200k for a couple and say that is a lot of money, but realistically its not all that much - we're certainly not talking about millionaires. A 2025 study by SmartAsset showed that for a family of four to live comfortably, they need a household income well above that: $290,368. Further, as a income tax credit would this not lead to a greater redistribution of income by giving larger refunds to those that pay little to no taxes to begin with?

Instead, lets start by reducing spending (so we're not just shifting one tax to another), and then lower some of the multitude of taxes in a way that would benefit us all - maybe the sales tax or the income tax itself. While we're at it, lets encourage Connecticut legislators to stay in their lane. Municipalities set their own budgets, the residents voting on those measures should be the ones coming up with the funds for those budgets and leave the state out of it. As I mentioned at the start of this letter, property taxes are just about the only means towns and cities have to raise revenue from their residents. Car taxes are additionally just about the only skin in the game that renters have. This may be an unpopular opinion, but someone that does not have skin in the game in a particular area should not have a say in that area's budget - just like I should have no say on the budgets of Bridgeport, East Haddam, or even NYC.

Thank you for allowing me the time to express my concerns on this, and for the great work you are doing in representing our needs in the state legislature.

Dear State Representative,

I am writing as a constituent to request your assistance with a serious procedural issue involving the Connecticut State Police Special Licensing and Firearms Unit (SLFU) and the handling of an out‑of‑state Extreme Risk Protection Order (ERPO). The situation has exposed a gap in Connecticut’s administrative process that leaves residents without any clear due‑process pathway to correct their records once an out‑of‑state ERPO has expired.

In my case, an ERPO was issued in another state and later expired by operation of law. Despite this, the Connecticut State Police treated the matter as a revocation rather than a temporary suspension tied to the ERPO’s duration. When I contacted SLFU for clarification, I received conflicting and inaccurate information, including statements that contradicted the statutory framework. At no point was I provided with a lawful or practical mechanism to restore my status after the ERPO expired.

The core problem is that Connecticut’s current procedures do not contemplate how to process the expiration of an ERPO issued by another state. As a result, residents are left in administrative limbo, with no statutory remedy, no appeal process, and no clear path to reinstatement. This is not simply a personal inconvenience — it is a structural failure that affects any Connecticut resident who becomes subject to an out‑of‑state ERPO, regardless of outcome.

I am requesting your assistance in bringing this matter to the attention of the appropriate committees or agencies. At minimum, Connecticut needs a clear, uniform process for:

Recognizing the expiration of an out‑of‑state ERPO

Correctly classifying the status of affected residents

Providing a defined pathway for reinstatement

Ensuring that SLFU applies the law consistently and accurately

I would appreciate any support you can provide in addressing this issue. I am available to supply documentation or speak further if needed.

Thank you for your time and attention.

During the 2025 legislative session, CT House Bill #7053 establishing a working group to develop uniform statutory definitions of “first responder” and “essential worker” passed both the House and Senate unanimously.  On July 8, 2025, Governor Lamont signed this Bill, designating is as Special Act 25-24.

I am again asking for your support to designate emergency telecommunicators, also known as 911 dispatchers, as “first responders” in the State of Connecticut.  Twenty-six states have passed legislation, in most cases unanimously, to enact this designation, including New York and New Jersey.  

Emergency telecommunicators are often the initial first responder the public encounters in an emergency.  We are trained and certified to provide lifesaving pre-arrival medical instruction to callers reporting medical emergencies including: traumatic injury, cardiac arrest, overdoes, suicide attempts, and vehicle accidents with injuries.  We are trained to walk callers through CPR over the phone when needed.  We receive specialized training in handling critical incidents including: domestic violence, hostage negotiation, sexual assault, human trafficking, bomb threats, crisis intervention, and active shooter incidents.

Emergency telecommunicators are charged with determining the location of an emergency, gathering information from callers to determine the level and type of response needed, relaying that information to responding field units (police/fire/ems), and continually updating responding field units with vital information as situations rapidly change.

During my career, I have coached multiple callers through CPR, assisted in the delivery of 2 healthy babies, talked to numerous suicidal callers, assisted numerous victims of domestic violence, assisted during missing children calls, the list of incidents could be several thousand pages long.

Emergency telecommunicators are dedicated public safety professionals who make a difference everyday to keep our communities and fellow first responders safe, please consider supporting this cause.

Sincerely,

During the 2025 legislative session, CT House Bill #7053 establishing a working group to develop uniform statutory definitions of “first responder” and “essential worker” passed both the House and Senate unanimously.  On July 8, 2025, Governor Lamont signed this Bill, designating is as Special Act 25-24.

I am again asking for your support to designate emergency telecommunicators, also known as 911 dispatchers, as “first responders” in the State of Connecticut.  Twenty-six states have passed legislation, in most cases unanimously, to enact this designation, including New York and New Jersey.  

Emergency telecommunicators are often the initial first responder the public encounters in an emergency.  We are trained and certified to provide lifesaving pre-arrival medical instruction to callers reporting medical emergencies including: traumatic injury, cardiac arrest, overdoes, suicide attempts, and vehicle accidents with injuries.  We are trained to walk callers through CPR over the phone when needed.  We receive specialized training in handling critical incidents including: domestic violence, hostage negotiation, sexual assault, human trafficking, bomb threats, crisis intervention, and active shooter incidents.

Emergency telecommunicators are charged with determining the location of an emergency, gathering information from callers to determine the level and type of response needed, relaying that information to responding field units (police/fire/ems), and continually updating responding field units with vital information as situations rapidly change.

During my career, I have coached multiple callers through CPR, assisted in the delivery of 2 healthy babies, talked to numerous suicidal callers, assisted numerous victims of domestic violence, assisted during missing children calls, the list of incidents could be several thousand pages long.

Emergency telecommunicators are dedicated public safety professionals who make a difference everyday to keep our communities and fellow first responders safe, please consider supporting this cause.

Sincerely,

Re: Please Sponsor The Family Rights and Due Process Act

Dear Representative Buchsbaum,

I write to urge your support for The Family Rights and Due Process Act. This bill is designed to protect children and strengthen due process in Connecticut family courts.

Under current law, most family cases in Connecticut are decided under the “preponderance of the evidence” standard. In plain English, that means a parent can lose custody or face restrictions if the judge believes the allegations are just slightly more likely true than not just 51 percent. See Fish v. Fish, 285 Conn. 24, 42 (2008) (custody determined by preponderance unless statute requires more). This standard applies in custody and visitation under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46b-56, support proceedings under § 46b-84, and modifications under § 46b-86. For restraining orders, the same “more likely than not” standard is used. See Putman v. Kennedy, 279 Conn. 162, 168 (2006). These statutes and cases make clear that even the most serious restrictions on a parent-child relationship can be imposed on bare majority evidence.

The Family Rights and Due Process Act would raise the standard to “clear and convincing evidence” in suits affecting the parent-child relationship, except where a higher standard already applies. It would also require judges to issue written findings of fact and conclusions of law that identify the evidence relied on and the legal basis for each ruling. If a court fails to file those findings within 10 business days, the case would be automatically reversible on appeal, giving families an enforceable safeguard.

This reform benefits children by ensuring that custody, visitation, and support orders are grounded in reliable evidence rather than marginal proof. Families will better understand judicial decisions, reducing appeals and mistrust. False allegations and perjury are discouraged when the law demands clear and convincing evidence and requires judges to explain their rulings in writing. The bill is cost-neutral: it does not add new procedures but simply raises the reliability of decisions and requires the court to issue findings it already has authority to provide under Practice Book § 64-1.

I respectfully request a 15- to 30-minute Zoom call to discuss sponsorship. Please help safeguard Connecticut children by sponsoring The Family Rights and Due Process Act.

The Family Rights and Due Process Act

CONNECTICUT STATE LEGISLATURE
[Filed by]
[Bill No]

Section 1. Findings and purpose
(1) The General Assembly finds that parental rights are a fundamental liberty interest under the Constitution.
(2) Reliable fact finding is essential to protect children and families.
(3) Material restrictions on the parent-child relationship shall not be imposed without clear and convincing evidence.

Sec. 2. Standard of proof in family matters
(a) A new section is added to chapter 815j of the General Statutes:

“Sec. [New]. (a) Except as otherwise provided by law, issues of fact in any proceeding under chapters 815j to 815y involving custody, visitation, child support, modification, parentage, or enforcement shall be determined by clear and convincing evidence.

(b) Nothing in this section reduces any higher burden of proof required by statute or case law.”

Sec. 3. Protective orders
Section 46b-15 of the General Statutes is amended to substitute “clear and convincing evidence” for “preponderance of the evidence” in the evidentiary standard for issuing a restraining order.

Sec. 4. Conforming amendments
(a) Custody and visitation determinations under § 46b-56 shall be made by clear and convincing evidence.
(b) Child support and deviations under § 46b-84 shall require clear and convincing evidence.
(c) Modifications under § 46b-86 shall require clear and convincing evidence of a substantial change in circumstances.
(d) Enforcement proceedings in civil contempt shall require clear and convincing evidence, provided that criminal contempt remains governed by the beyond a reasonable doubt standard.
(e) Parentage adjudications under § 46b-160 shall require clear and convincing evidence where civil standards apply.

Sec. 5. Written findings of fact and conclusions of law
(a) The court shall issue written findings of fact and conclusions of law in any case decided under the clear and convincing standard.
(b) Such findings shall identify the evidence relied on and the legal basis for each material ruling.
(c) Findings shall be filed not later than 10 business days after the signing of the order.

Sec. 6. Enforcement for failure to file findings
Failure to file the required findings and conclusions within thirty days results in automatic reversal on appeal. The aggrieved party shall have an automatic right of appeal, and the appellate court shall remand for new proceedings consistent with this Act.

Sec. 7. Effective date
This Act takes effect January 1, 202?, and applies to cases filed on or after that date and to orders entered on or after that date.

Sec. 8. Severability
If any provision of this Act is held invalid, the remainder shall not be affected. This section is declaratory of existing law under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-3.

BACKGROUND AND NEED FOR THE BILL
In Connecticut, parents depend on the courts to ensure that court-ordered parenting time is respected and enforced. Yet in many cases, one parent unilaterally denies access to the other without legal justification, leaving the child deprived of time with a loving parent and the wronged parent without a clear remedy.

Current enforcement statutes allow courts to address contempt but do not guarantee make-up time for parenting time wrongfully denied. This often leads to prolonged litigation, emotional harm to the child, and erosion of parental trust in the legal system.

The Time Taken, Time Back Act corrects this problem by ensuring that parenting time is not just ordered—but protected and restored. It creates a clear and fair rule: if court-ordered time is taken away without good cause, that time must be returned.

This bill:

Protects the child’s right to maintain relationships with both parents
Reduces parental gatekeeping and interference
Creates judicial consistency and accountability
Deters false allegations and frivolous denials
Provides relief without the need for modification proceedings
By passing this legislation, Connecticut affirms its commitment to family stability, judicial integrity, and the protection of parental rights.

BILL NO. [TO BE ASSIGNED]

A BILL FOR AN ACT
CONCERNING COMPENSATORY PARENTING TIME FOR WRONGFUL DENIAL OF COURT-ORDERED ACCESS.


SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act shall be known and may be cited as the “Connecticut Time Taken, Time Back Act.”


SECTION 2. CONNECTICUT GENERAL STATUTES, TITLE 46B (FAMILY LAW), IS AMENDED TO ADD:
Sec. 46b-56g. Compensatory Parenting Time for Denial of Court-Ordered Access.
(a) Authority of the Court.
 If a court finds that a parent has been wrongfully denied court-ordered parenting time, the court shall order compensatory parenting time to make up for the time denied, unless the denying parent shows good cause.

(b) Presumption.
 There shall be a rebuttable presumption that compensatory time is warranted if:
(1) The parenting time denial was not authorized by court order; and
(2) The denial was not based on a substantiated finding of abuse, neglect, or other imminent risk to the child by any investigative agency.

(c) Scheduling and Enforcement.
 (1) Make-up parenting time shall be of the same type and duration as the time wrongfully denied.
(2) The denied parent may select dates for the make-up time within six months of the denial, subject to the child’s best interest and school schedule.
(3) Compensatory time shall take precedence over non-court-ordered extracurricular or social activities.
(4) If a pattern of three or more violations occurs within a 24-month period, the court may modify custody or impose additional sanctions.

(d) Application.
 This section applies to all final orders, temporary orders, and enforcement proceedings related to parenting time under Chapter 815j.


SECTION 3. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act takes effect on October 1, 2026, and applies to all cases filed or pending on or after that date.

Dear State Representative Bronko, 
 
As the legislative session begins, Care-at-Home providers in Connecticut urge you to make Medicaid funding for in-home services a top priority. Recent federal budget and policy changes have further exposed a provider system that is already dangerously underfunded. Medicaid rates that fail to reflect the true cost of care threaten the stability of home-based agencies and jeopardize access to essential services for our state’s most vulnerable residents—delivered in the setting they overwhelmingly prefer: their own homes.
 
Without decisive action to adequately fund Medicaid home care, thousands of seniors face the loss of critical in-home supports, forcing unnecessary nursing facility placements and driving avoidable hospitalizations—outcomes that are more costly to the state and more disruptive to the lives of those we serve.
 
As part of my role at Masonicare I sit on countless risk meetings for patients who are in dire circumstances, have needs that far outstrip their ability to meet them, and often have no other resources financially or socially to maintain their health, safety, and human dignity. Medicaid is critical to maintaining health, safety, and human dignity for these people.  The ability for people to remain in their homes not only enhances their quality of life but also saves money in the long run, without the in-home care that Medicaid enables, most of these people would have no other choice than to reside in a skilled nursing facility or care home at a much greater expense to Medicaid. 
 
Here is our Medicaid funding ask:

•	Licensed home health agencies: 10% each year for the next five years

•	Homemaker-companion agencies: 13% each of the next two years, then 10% each of the next three years
 
Care-at-Home providers can’t wait any longer. Fund Home Care to meet the true costs of care and maintain the human dignity we all deserve. 
 
Thank you for your leadership and for your commitment to supporting the residents and caregivers who rely on care at home.
 
Kind Regards,
Helena Vieira, RN, BSN, MSN
Associate Executive Director of Home Health
Masonicare Home Health & Hospice
Resident of Naugatuck, CT

Dear Representative Marra,

I am a resident of Darien, a UnitedHealthcare member, and the parent of young children who receive primary and specialty care through Stamford Health. Stamford Hospital is also the closest emergency department for my family.

I am writing to express serious concern about the ongoing contract dispute between UnitedHealthcare and Stamford Health and to urge state leadership to actively mediate this situation before patient access is disrupted.

Both organizations have released statements focused on costs, benchmarks, and financial sustainability. What is largely missing from this public debate is accountability for patients—particularly families with children, people with chronic conditions, and those who rely on Stamford Hospital as their nearest emergency room.

If Stamford Health goes out of network, the impact will not be theoretical. Thousands of patients will be displaced in an already capacity-constrained region. Nearby hospitals and specialists cannot realistically absorb this volume without significant increases in wait times, delayed care, and reduced access to timely emergency and specialty services. This is not simply an inconvenience; it is a patient safety issue.

As a parent, I am deeply concerned about continuity of care. My children’s doctors know their histories. Our primary care and specialty relationships are not easily or quickly replaced. In an emergency, families should not have to weigh network status against proximity and urgency.

I am not writing to take sides in a financial negotiation. I am asking the state to step in on behalf of patients—who have no seat at the negotiating table—to ensure:

Active mediation between the parties

Transparency around the real access and capacity implications of a contract termination

Good evening,

Thank you both so much for your time this morning! It was nice talking to you and giving an update on the current issues APRNs face in CT.

I found a quick summary on the CTAPRNS Website:

-Collaboration for New Graduate APRNs

Currently the state of Connecticut requires a new graduate APRN to have a collaborative agreement with a physician for 3 years and 2000 hours. This requirement is not evidence based and none of our surrounding states require this (NY, MA, RI, ME, NH).
Solution: Update language to allow for new graduate APRNs to collaborate with experienced APRNs.

 -Reciprocity for APRNs from Other States

Currently an experienced APRN from a different state would need a new collaborative agreement with a physician in order to practice in Connecticut. This is a barrier for many APRNs that want to work in Connecticut or open practices.
Solution: Update language to allow for experienced APRNs from other states to practice without a collaborative agreement if they have met the practice requirements.

 -Global Signature

Currently numerous Connecticut statutes and regulations were written before APRNs were in practice and do not list APRNs, despite their current scope of practice and training. This omits APRNs from signing forms for the care that they provide.
Solution: Update language to allow for global signature authority for all forms or procedures within the current training and scope of practice of APRNs.

-Regulation Updates

Numerous regulations use language specific to physicians regarding staffing and responsibilities, regardless of the qualifications of APRNs. These regulations cross various departments including DSS, DPH, and DMHAS. The regulatory process in Connecticut can be difficult to update.
Solution: Continue to advocate for inter-professional updates to outdated regulations in order to reflect the qualifications of APRNs and to practice at the full extent of their training.

I hope this helps and feel free to reach out to us if you have any questions!

Sincerely,
Heather Gatesman, APRN & Kathleen Sullivan, APRN

Subject: Proposal to allow twin siblings to ride together during teen driver probation period

Matthew and Tyler Medina

1 Clarkson Lane

Killingworth, CT



Dear Senator Stephen Harding,



As High School freshman twins, we are writing to respectfully request your consideration for a modest, but meaningful amendment to Connecticut’s teen driving laws-specifically, to allow twin siblings to drive together during the six-month passenger restriction period that follows the issuance of a driver’s license to 16 and 17 year olds.

Under current Connecticut law (CGS § 14-36g), newly licensed teen drivers are prohibited from transporting any passengers besides a parent, legal guardian, or qualified adult for the first six months. While I fully support the intent of this law to enhance teen driver safety, it overlooks unique family circumstances—especially that of twins who are the same age and often share school, work, and extracurricular schedules.



I propose that the law be amended to include an exemption allowing a newly licensed teen driver to transport their twin sibling under the following conditions:



The sibling is a biological or legal twin (born within 12 months of the driver);
The trip is directly to or from school, work, medical appointments, or extracurricular activities;
Both siblings are properly licensed and/or seatbelted;
Neither has any history of moving violations or license suspensions;
The exemption would not apply to unrelated minors or general peers.


This change would greatly reduce the financial burden of parents purchasing two vehicles, redundant car trips, ease the burden on working parents, and promote environmental efficiency without compromising the core intent of the current law. In fact, twins often act as built-in accountability partners, providing mutual support rather than distraction.


I believe this thoughtful exception balances safety with the realities many families face and reflects a common-sense update to existing legislation. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this proposal further and appreciate your time and consideration.


Thank you for your public service and your attention to this issue.



Sincerely,

Tyler Medina

Matthew Medina

Greater flexibility in the application of the September 1 cutoff rule

Hi Senator, we spoke briefly Friday but, I wanted to share in detail Austin's full story with you.  Please let me know if you need more information or have any questions. 

I am writing to seek your advice, perspective, and any guidance you may be willing to offer as I begin legislative and policy efforts within our state to prevent other families from enduring what my family has experienced.

In November 2024, my former husband and I were wrongfully arrested by the Bristol Police and charged with felony child abuse following allegations related to injuries observed in our infant son, Austin. Austin was conceived after a three-year battle with infertility, following a tubal pregnancy and miscarriage. Becoming a mother was not incidental for me—it was a goal I pursued with determination, medical guidance, and profound personal sacrifice.

In the summer of 2022, after years of unsuccessful attempts to conceive, I was informed that medical intervention would not be considered unless I significantly improved my health. I committed to a complete lifestyle transformation, losing over 100 pounds, working with weight loss counselors, and radically changing my diet and daily habits. After reaching the required medical threshold, I began medicated fertility cycles, followed by months of intensive treatment, monitoring, and ultimately my first IUI. Austin’s conception was the result of sustained effort, medical oversight, and unwavering intent to become his mother.

From birth, I consistently brought Austin to his pediatrician for routine care and repeatedly raised concerns about bruising, particularly in light of his traumatic birth. At the recommendation of his pediatrician, I brought Austin to the hospital for X-rays when he was two months old in November of 2023. These images revealed fractures that were deemed “unexplained,” which resulted in his immediate removal from our home, criminal charges against us, and involvement with the Department of Children and Families. Austin was removed from our care on November 16, 2023.

Following these events, and after several failed specialist appointments at Yale and Connecticut Children’s Medical Center, I sought comprehensive medical evaluations for both Austin and myself at Boston University. We were each diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS), a genetic connective tissue disorder known to increase susceptibility to bruising and fractures. Based on these medical findings, all criminal charges were fully dismissed by the New Britain Court in the summer of 2025.

Despite this clear medical explanation and the dismissal of criminal charges, the Department of Children and Families has stated that it does not recognize Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome as a medical cause of Austin’s injuries. As a result, I still do not have full custody of my son. Austin was without the full care of his mother for 612 days, despite the absence of criminal findings and the presence of documented medical explanations. While a transfer of guardianship to his paternal grandmother has allowed Austin to return to our care, this arrangement is neither appropriate nor acceptable as a long-term solution.

I am now advocating for policy reform to ensure that medically documented genetic and rare conditions are appropriately recognized during child welfare investigations. Families who proactively seek medical care, follow pediatric recommendations, and act in good faith should not be criminalized or separated for extended periods when credible medical evidence exists. Also, families should be able to be given the right to second options. 

I would greatly value your thoughts on this issue and welcome any advice you may have on how best to advance these efforts. In particular, I am seeking guidance on potential legislative or policy solutions such as:
- Requiring child welfare agencies to consult qualified medical specialists when rare or genetic conditions are suspected
- Ensuring due process protections for families when criminal charges have been dismissed based on medical findings
- Improving training and medical guidance for child protection investigators regarding connective tissue disorders such as EDS
- Establishing oversight or review mechanisms when agency determinations conflict with established medical diagnoses

Your leadership and commitment to supporting mothers and families could make a meaningful difference in preventing similar harm to other families. I would welcome the opportunity to meet, share medical documentation, and discuss possible paths forward.

Thank you very much for your time, consideration, and dedication to protecting children and families in our state.  Please let me know next steps, and If you can assist with this matter.

Connecticut Voters Made their Choice, Now The Legislature
Needs to Act

In 2024 Connecticut voters overwhelmingly approved Question 1, a constitutional amendment removing the requirement that voters needed an excuse to vote by absentee ballot. With that vote, Connecticut joined 37 other states that allow absentee voting for all. And the results were decisive. It was a clear directive from the people of this state to the Legislature: modernize our elections and give voters more flexibility to cast their ballots from home.

Yet as lawmakers move to implement what voters already approved, false claims about fraud, untethered from evidence are resurfacing. These claims deserve a careful, fact-based response, especially when they risk delaying or undermining the will of the people.

Election fraud of any kind is extremely uncommon in the United States, and is a felony in most states. Multiple studies, bipartisan election officials, and court rulings across the country have found fraud rates measured not in percentages, but in fractions of a fraction of a percent.

The National Vote at Home Institute (NVAHI) has studied state voting systems, including those where every active voter is automatically delivered a ballot to their doorstep. Greater access to mail ballots increases voter participation across all demographic groups, with no partisan advantage. Utah, Colorado, and Oregon, all universal Vote at Home states, consistently lead the nation in voter participation.

Other states with no-excuse absentee voting have also seen their participation rates go up. Voting by mail is good for all voters but especially for working families, voters with childcare and eldercare responsibilities, seniors, disabled voters, and young people.

In a properly designed voting system, mail ballots are not postcards floating freely through the system. They are part of a tightly controlled, multi-step process designed to protect ballot secrecy and prevent tampering. In fact, mail ballots are among the safest and most secure voting methods available: each ballot carries a unique barcode, ballot delivery can be tracked online by voters, and “curing” ensures small mistakes don’t silence voters’ voices.

Those who charge that mail ballots are not secure undermine confidence in elections, without proof, and discourage participation, erode trust, and weaken the very foundations of self-government.

If mail voting were truly vulnerable to widespread fraud, it would show up in audits, recounts, prosecutions, or overturned elections. It hasn’t. Those who actually run elections, Republican and Democratic officials alike, have repeatedly affirmed that mail voting is safe, secure, and reliable.

Mail ballots are secure. Our democracy is stronger when we say so. clearly, confidently, and without apology. Implementing a robust and efficient system, with strong safeguards and transparent processes, honors both the Constitution and our own common sense.

Connecticut voters were clear in 2024: They want the freedom to choose how they vote. Now it’s time for the legislature to honor the people’s will.

My name is Jason Chilly, and I am a 2011 HVAC graduate of Windham Technical High School. While Windham Tech had a significant influence on my life, this letter is not about me. It is about the future blue-collar workers who come from the Windham and Willimantic community.
During my time as a student, several classmates and I had the opportunity to have breakfast with State Representatives Tim Ackert and Susan Johnson. The central focus of that discussion was the importance of keeping the doors open at Windham Tech and the value the school provides to the region.
After graduating from Windham Tech, I was hired as a Firefighter/EMT with the Willimantic Fire Department. In addition to fire protection and emergency medical services, much of our work involves supporting residents with basic human and mental health needs—many of which are directly tied to poverty.
Years later, I reconnected with my former soccer coach, who spent more than 30 years positively impacting students lives. Through him, I was given the opportunity to return to Windham Tech as a coach and give back to the school and community that gave me so much.
Windham Tech serves the greater Willimantic area and functions as a hub of opportunity within one of the most economically challenged communities in Connecticut. Many of the students who attend the school come directly from Windham and Willimantic, where poverty affects nearly every aspect of daily life.
Through my work as a firefighter and EMT, I have entered hundreds, if not thousands, of homes in Windham. I have seen living conditions that most people passing through the community would never know exist. Children live in some of these homes.
When we talk about supporting vulnerable communities, we often focus on access to healthcare and food. Education and job training are just as critical.
As a coach, I saw firsthand how many students walked to and from school and after-school activities. Some parents lacked reliable transportation. Others worked long or multiple jobs, limiting their ability to provide consistent support. While these challenges can exist anywhere, I witnessed them most often right here in Windham.
Athletic and extracurricular programs help build discipline, teamwork, and character. More importantly, they provide structure, mentorship, and a reason for students to stay on track. Removing barriers to participation matters—especially for students who already face significant obstacles.
Moving Windham Tech out of walking distance from the community it serves would be a serious disservice to these children. For many students, Windham Tech represents stability, opportunity, and a pathway to a skilled career. It allows students with the odds stacked against them to gain hands-on, job-ready experience and build relationships with mentors who can help them navigate life’s challenges.
Relocating the school may have little impact on other sending communities, but it would have a profound impact on Windham. The students who rely on proximity, accessibility, and community connection would be affected the most.
As someone who has witnessed firsthand the benefits that Windham Tech’s current location provides, I respectfully ask that you do what is right for the children of the Windham community.
Please do not sever these children’s access to opportunity and stability.

Hi Representative Scott and team,

I’m a constituent in Monroe, Connecticut, and I’m writing to ask you to support legislation that protects grocery staples from algorithmic or individualized “dynamic pricing,” especially online and in stores using digital shelf labels.

Recent reporting based on a Consumer Reports + Groundwork Collaborative investigation found that Instacart showed different prices to different shoppers for the same items at the same store and time—without clear disclosure (see 1 and 2). Walmart recently began to remove price tags and switching to digital price display (see 3). I’m reaching out because I believe staple foods should be protected from this kind of pricing practice.

By background, I’m a senior-level data scientist at Indeed, and I’m also a mom of two little kids. I’m very familiar with how experimentation and algorithmic decision systems work in practice—and how easy it is for them to create real harm when applied to essentials or when their results are misinterpreted.

Why staples are special:
Staples like eggs, milk, and bread have relatively inelastic demand (see 4). Families don’t have real flexibility to “opt out” when prices shift, and substitutes are limited—especially when you’re shopping for kids and trying to keep a household running. In that environment, algorithmic price changes can function like a quiet, unavoidable tax on basic life needs.

Small per-item changes are effectively invisible at decision time:
A 10–20 cent change on a staple item often won’t affect whether someone buys it in that moment. But across a full basket, those small changes can add up quickly—without the shopper ever making an informed choice (see 5). This is exactly the kind of mechanism that can transfer significant money from families to companies while staying below the threshold of what people can realistically notice, compare, or respond to during a normal shopping trip.

Experimentation at scale can create misleading “wins”:
As someone who runs experiments professionally, I’m also concerned that companies can mistakenly treat short-term revenue lifts from dynamic pricing experiments as “proof” a practice is good or fair. When you run many experiments simultaneously and optimize locally, you increase the risk of false positives and overfitting—especially if guardrails like multiple-testing controls and long-term impact measurement aren’t in place (see 6). The result is a system that can look successful on dashboards while producing negative long-term effects: reduced trust, higher household financial stress, and broader economic drag.

My request:

I’m not trying to stop normal sales, coupons, or transparent price competition. I’m asking for a basic consumer protection principle for staple foods: one posted price, not individualized or rapidly fluctuating algorithmic pricing—plus clear disclosure and enforceable rules when algorithms are used.

If helpful, I would support any of the following policy approaches:
- A ban or strict limits on algorithmic/individualized pricing for a defined list of staple foods (eggs, milk, bread, infant formula, etc.).
- A “price stability” requirement for staples (e.g., no more than one change per a set period (e.g. 24 hours to 3 days), and no cart-to-checkout price changes).
- Clear disclosure requirements when algorithmic pricing is used, paired with audit authority and enforcement by the Attorney General / consumer protection agency.

Thank you for your time and for representing our community. I would appreciate hearing whether you are considering legislation in this area, and who on your staff I should follow up with. Kindly leave a voicemail if calling (I receive an unusually high volume of spam calls).

Sincerely,
Viyaleta Apgar

Monroe, CT

(203) 752-7172
viyaleta.apgar@gmail.com

On October 14, 2025, I contacted Access Health and spoke with Tracy. I explained that I only have Medicare Part A (hospital coverage). She informed me that I was not eligible for Medicaid because my husband and I filed our taxes separately. She also stated that I did not qualify because I am on Medicare, and suggested that I apply for Husky C for adults with disabilities. I explained that this seemed unnecessary, as she was simultaneously telling me I would not qualify due to having Medicare Part A. It became clear that I needed to apply for Medicare Part B.

 

On November 7, 2025, I called Medicare and was emailed an application for Part B. I faxed the completed application on November 12, 2025. On November 22, 2025, Social Security mailed me a request for additional information, which I faxed back on November 25, 2025.

 

On November 26, 2025, I contacted Access Health again to confirm that my coverage would in fact end on November 30. I was then transferred to Social Services, where I was told to apply for Husky C, and was informed that I might still qualify even though I have Medicare. This was confusing, as I was not told this in October by Access Health. DSS explained that Access Health would not have been aware to advise me of that option.

 

Despite this, I am certain that I would not qualify, as my husband’s income and our assets would be counted due to our marital status.

 

I then contacted Social Security and spoke with Michelle, who informed me that I will likely be subject to a lifelong penalty because I did not enroll in Medicare Part B in 2021, when I had coverage through Husky/Medicaid. This was the first time I was ever told that choosing not to enroll would result in a permanent penalty. If declining Part B results in a lifetime fine, it is not truly an “option.” She also informed me that I am not eligible to apply for Part B until the General Enrollment Period in February.

 

This has left me extremely confused. Access Health and DSS are stating that I am not eligible for Medicaid because I have Medicare, yet I do not have full Medicare coverage, and cannot obtain it until February. As a result, I am now without comprehensive coverage for several months. It is difficult to understand how it is appropriate to terminate a disabled person’s health insurance and leave them unable to obtain necessary medical care.

 

Additionally, I am confused regarding the rules on taxes, filing status, and eligibility. When I called Access Health on October 5, 2022, Jessica and Karissa informed me that if my husband and I filed taxes separately, he did not need to be included on my application. I was specifically told, “If filing taxes in 2023 for 2022 married filing separately, your husband does not need to be on the application.” Yet in 2025, I am now being told that filing separately is one of the reasons I do not qualify.

 

Overall, the system has been extremely confusing. It appears that the various state agencies do not have consistent information, and I have repeatedly received conflicting guidance. At this time, I understand that I only have Medicare Part A hospital coverage and possibly prescription coverage. I cannot apply for full Medicare coverage until February, and I may face a lifetime penalty—despite having acted based on the information I was given.

 

If the agencies responsible for administering these programs cannot provide consistent and accurate information, it is difficult to understand how individuals like myself are expected to navigate these processes or maintain necessary health coverage.

Good Morning/Afternoon Representative Zullo,

I hope my email finds you well….my name is Tod Van Kirk and I am responsible for the programming that is offered by Aspire Living and Learning in Connecticut (formerly the Institute of Professional Practice (IPPI)), a large, multi-state provider of services to neurodiverse adults. 

If you are unfamiliar with Aspire, we offer adults life-long services mostly, though not exclusively, through the “group home” (CLA/ICF) model of service delivery for those with disabilities. We partner with the Department of Developmental Services (DDS), the Department of Social Services (DSS) and others in the coordination and delivery of our services.

I am writing today to both invite you to visit one of our programs, and for two additional reasons…

First, to acknowledge the work during the previous legislature which resulted in an increase in reimbursement rates for Medicaid service providers and the passing (and subsequent signature of the Governor) of Substitute Senate Bill 1358, now Public Act 25-151 which, among other things, ties future reimbursement rates for providers to increases to the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Second, to bring forward the following two issues that persist, despite the recent effort detailed above, that will ultimately have the unintended consequence of Aspire needing to shutter several of the homes we have operated for years, causing traumatic impact to the lives of those we provide services to, and, to our dedicated employees:

1.	While the recent efforts to increase funding helps some, unfortunately, overall reimbursement rates for Community Living Arrangements (commonly referred to as CLA’s, or “group homes”) continue to fall short of covering the ongoing cost of service delivery for providers.  Furthermore, the room and board rates for CLA’s (which are funded through DSS) fall dramatically short of expenses incurred. This is primarily due to the lack of rate increases over the previous 20-year period. As a result of this historical backlog, providers like Aspire continue to lose money on the services we deliver. To quantify this cumulative deficit in funding, the Connecticut Nonprofit Alliance notes; - after the rate increases and the new legislation - community nonprofits continue to operate with 30% less buying power than in 2007. Simply put, Aspire needs additional funding to cover continuing losses in the form of higher rates of reimbursement for services provided.

2.	In addition to the operation of CLA’s, Aspire Living and Learning understands the need - and accepts the risk and responsibility - for operating DSS funded Intermediate Care Facilities (ICF’s) for adults with disabilities – which are classified as “nursing homes” in Connecticut. Residents of these homes require a significantly higher level of care. Two main issues exist for providers operating ICF’s. First, established rates do not come anywhere close to covering the operational and care-based costs and second, in simple terms, as “nursing facilities”, financials for ICF’s are reported to DSS, while financials for CLA’s are reported to DDS. Currently, these two agencies will not view the cumulative financials of these two service lines. This siloed approach, coupled with the DDS “revenue retention” rule (which, with a few exceptions, requires reported surpluses be given back to the state) puts undo strain on a service provider operating as one agency with one set of expenses. We seek relief from this standard and request the legislature acts to change the requirements of the respective state departments (DDS/DSS) allowing one services’ potential surplus to cover the loss in another – just as DDS does with all of their respective service lines. After all, there is only one Medicaid authority in the state (DSS).

Please let me know when you are available to discuss these issues and/or to come visit one of our programs - we would be honored to host you.

Thank you again for all that you do for the citizens of Connecticut.

Respectfully,
Tod Van Kirk
Senior Director of Adult Services
State of Connecticut

If you are unfamiliar with Aspire, we offer adults life-long services mostly, though not exclusively, through the “group home” (CLA/ICF) model of service delivery for those with disabilities. We partner with the Department of Developmental Services (DDS), the Department of Social Services (DSS) and others in the coordination and delivery of our services.

I am writing today to both invite you to visit one of our programs, and for two additional reasons…

First, to acknowledge the work during the previous legislature which resulted in an increase in reimbursement rates for Medicaid service providers and the passing (and subsequent signature of the Governor) of Substitute Senate Bill 1358, now Public Act 25-151 which, among other things, ties future reimbursement rates for providers to increases to the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Second, to bring forward the following two issues that persist, despite the recent effort detailed above, that will ultimately have the unintended consequence of Aspire needing to shutter several of the homes we have operated for years, causing traumatic impact to the lives of those we provide services to, and, to our dedicated employees:

1.	While the recent efforts to increase funding helps some, unfortunately, overall reimbursement rates for Community Living Arrangements (commonly referred to as CLA’s, or “group homes”) continue to fall short of covering the ongoing cost of service delivery for providers.  Furthermore, the room and board rates for CLA’s (which are funded through DSS) fall dramatically short of expenses incurred. This is primarily due to the lack of rate increases over the previous 20-year period. As a result of this historical backlog, providers like Aspire continue to lose money on the services we deliver. To quantify this cumulative deficit in funding, the Connecticut Nonprofit Alliance notes; - after the rate increases and the new legislation - community nonprofits continue to operate with 30% less buying power than in 2007. Simply put, Aspire needs additional funding to cover continuing losses in the form of higher rates of reimbursement for services provided.

2.	In addition to the operation of CLA’s, Aspire Living and Learning understands the need - and accepts the risk and responsibility - for operating DSS funded Intermediate Care Facilities (ICF’s) for adults with disabilities – which are classified as “nursing homes” in Connecticut. Residents of these homes require a significantly higher level of care. Two main issues exist for providers operating ICF’s. First, established rates do not come anywhere close to covering the operational and care-based costs and second, in simple terms, as “nursing facilities”, financials for ICF’s are reported to DSS, while financials for CLA’s are reported to DDS. Currently, these two agencies will not view the cumulative financials of these two service lines. This siloed approach, coupled with the DDS “revenue retention” rule (which, with a few exceptions, requires reported surpluses be given back to the state) puts undo strain on a service provider operating as one agency with one set of expenses. We seek relief from this standard and request the legislature acts to change the requirements of the respective state departments (DDS/DSS) allowing one services’ potential surplus to cover the loss in another – just as DDS does with all of their respective service lines. After all, there is only one Medicaid authority in the state (DSS).

Please let me know when you are available to discuss these issues and/or to come visit one of our programs - we would be honored to host you.

Thank you again for all that you do for the citizens of Connecticut.

Respectfully,
Tod Van Kirk
Senior Director of Adult Services
State of Connecticut
