Connecticut General Statutes Title 47A. Landlord and Tenant § 47a-13. Failure of landlord to supply essential services.

Heat -- Provided to Tenants

 

If renters have no heat, they should call local police and their local health department. The requirement for landlords to provide heat when it is included as part of the rental agreement is enforced by cities and towns. 

State law says that if the landlord is required to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or other essential service to tenants, and if the landlord fails to supply such essential service, and the failure is not caused by conditions beyond the landlord’s control, the tenant may give notice to the landlord specifying the breach and may elect to procure reasonable amounts of essential services during the period of non-compliance and deduct the actual and reasonable cost of such service from the rent.

The tenant may instead choose to procure reasonable substitute housing during the period of the landlord’s non-compliance if the landlord fails to supply such service within 2 business days of such breach. 

If the landlord fails to provide the same service a second time within 6 months, the tenant may secure substitute housing immediately. 

If the landlord willfully fails to provide an essential service, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement and recover an amount not more than two months' rent or double the actual damages sustained by him, whichever is greater.

I am writing to you today about a very important topic that I think needs to be addressed in our society for Rare Disease Week. Many individuals with rare diseases go through the long process of gaining a diagnosis which is known as the “diagnostic odyssey”. For individuals living with rare diseases, this “diagnostic odyssey” often lasts five to seven years, during which patients and families endure repeated specialist visits, unnecessary testing, misdiagnoses, emotional and financial hardship. These delays aren’t just inconvenient—they can lead to irreversible health complications, prevent early interventions, and place enormous strain on families who often lose work hours and stability in the process. Although rare diseases affect a small number of people, they are still human and deserve what is right for them. Early and accurate diagnosis is both life-saving and cost-saving. For example, when conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) are identified early, timely treatment can prevent severe disability and dramatically reduce long-term healthcare expenses. We already have the tools that can shorten diagnostic delays, including genetic testing, more extensive newborn screening, and improved clinical diagnosing systems. What we need now is improved access, consistent insurance coverage, and federal support to ensure these resources reach families who are in need. Shortening the diagnostic odyssey will save lives, reduce healthcare costs, and give families and individuals the quality of life they deserve. With the right legislative action, we can ensure that every patient receives answers when they need them, not years too late.

Things are getting pretty busy at the Connecticut Insurance Department (CID).

As I reported last month, Genworth recently filed two premium increase requests, including one on my policy. On November 4, 2025, the CID announced three more new premium increase requests for three different companies.

Thanks for reading Long-Term Care Insurance Crisis! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Subscribed
In reviewing the Initial Filing documents filed by each carrier, they are listing the same usual issues;

· These are closed policies.

· People are living longer and therefore more people are going on claim.

· People are holding on to their policies longer than we anticipated which is leading to more claims.

But there is an interesting twist to this latest increase requests by John Hancock Life Insurance for their 4060 Policy Series.

The CID File Number is: 202505157, with a Filed Date of: 10/22/25

This request covers two policy forms;

· Form Number 4062-CT was sold from August 1997 to September 1998 (13 months). As of 12/31/2023, this form had 23 active policies.

· Form Number 4063-CT was sold from September 1997 to May 1999 (20 Months). As of 12/31/2023, this form had 54 active policies.

Based on the remaining policy counts, there are clearly not enough current policyholders, and probably never were, to generate enough premiums to cover the potential future claims.

The company is requesting a rate increase of 95.3% phased in with a maximum annual rate of 25% per year. That statement is misleading. Are they suggesting that they are only asking for a 75% increase (25% per year based on the current premium)? I think not. I did the math. What they will do is compound the rate increase so that while the rate increase looks like only 25% each year, in the second and third year they are getting 25% of the prior year’s increase.

However, the company is seeking to achieve a 100% loss ratio. In order to do that, they say they need a one-time 797.4% rate increase, so the company will be filing additional rate increases in the future. Nothing says to a policyholder, cancel your policy now while you still can, like the threat of an 800% premium increase.

But the facts and figures associated with this rate increase request is not what caught my attention. Rather, it is the fact that these policies were originally sold by Time Insurance Company (Time), a Wisconsin based company that was declared insolvent in 2020 and placed into rehabilitation.

John Hancock had been reinsuring the claims for Time for over 20-years and was also acting as the claim administrator. In June 2022, John Hancock assumed responsibility for about 25,000 Long-Term Care Insurance policies originally issued by Time. Everyone associated with this move seemed pretty proud of themselves saying that since John Hancock had already been administering these claims for years, policyholders probably wouldn’t even notice that their policies has changed hands.

Now, with Time no longer in the picture, John Hancock is stepping forward seeking a total rate increase of almost 800%.

According to the Initial Filing document published by the CID, the average premium for these two policy forms is about $5,700.00 per year. If these premiums increase by the suggested 797.4% mentioned by John Hancick, the average annual premium would be $51,174.

At that level, John Hancock is basically suggesting that these policyholders are insuring themselves.

It’s not clear from the documentation, or from my research whether John Hancock was forced to take over this business or whether they did so voluntarily. There is also no indication what level of reinsurance John Hancock provided to Time, or whether they (John Hancock) purchased their own reinsurance (known as a retrocession) for their own reimbursement.

Regardless, John Hancock knew, or should have known when they did their reinsurance underwriting that these policies were seriously underfunded and destined for financial failure. Why should the policyholders now bail them out for their prior poor decisions?

I have posted a formal comment to this rate filing which is below.

I object to this rate increase request.

The CID is on record saying that they do not consider reinsurance recoveries in their rate increase analysis because reinsurance was not considered in their original pricing analysis. They further stated that if the reinsurer is unable to fulfil its obligations, the original insurance company is still responsible for the claim payments.

Said another way, the CID is saying, as far as they are concerned, the reinsurer doesn’t exist and is not considered in their analysis.

Now, that John Hancock, who was the reinsurer, who by the way was already reimbursing Time for some or all of these claims, is now taking over for the original company, the CID is just going to treat them like the original company. And, if John Hancock has reinsurance on these claims, the CID going to ignore that because after all, they don’t consider reinsurance in their analysis.

It seems to me that the CID is once again doing whatever it can to help the industry at the expense of the policyholder.

If reinsurance recoveries should not be considered in the original company’s rate request, then the reinsurance company should not be allowed to suddenly step into that company’s shoes, just because they assumed this business.

Time Insurance clearly did not know how to price and manage their business. John Hancock clearly didn’t know how to evaluate their exposure when they agreed to reinsure Time’s Long-Term Care Insurance book of business for reinsurance purposes. The thought that the CID will now consider a 95% rate increase with the potential for a 797.4% increase in the future helps everyone’s financial problems, except for the policyholders.

The CID continues to forgive these companies for their errors and instead, keeps putting the burden on the policyholders, who were misled by the industry, at best, and outright lied to at worst, when they purchased these policies.

For these and other good and sufficient reasons, this rate request should be denied in its entirety.

I am writing to you out of concern for the Old Killingly Pond Dam, Killingly Connecticut.  Basically, the private owner of the dam, Wright Investors Service Holdings, does not want to be responsible or liable for the dam anymore.  The dam forms a Pond (one in a series) with a varied ecosystem that is home to bald eagles and a protected loon, as well as provides recreational opportunities (fishing, swimming, boating, kayaking, hunting) for the general public as part and parcel of Killingly State Park and forms the backyard of several private residents, some of whom who have held their properties for over a century.  
This past Sunday, October 26, 2025, Wright began lowering the pond’s water level.  According to a posting on the Town of Killingly Facebook page on that date, “This action was recommended by the dam owner’s engineer following recent monitoring that identified silt seepage.  Town officials emphasize that there is no immediate hazard to the public or property.  This release is being conducted out of an abundance of caution.  The Connecticut DEEP Dam Division has been notified, and the Town’s Emergency Management Director, Wetlands Agent, and Town Engineer are monitoring the situation.” I further understand that Wright has informed DEEP that it has no plans to repair or continue maintaining the dam.
Friends and residents of the Pond are seeking assistance in preserving and maintaining the dam and the Pond. We respectfully ask that you consider sponsoring a bill in the 2026 legislative session to fund and authorize the refurbishment of the Killingly Pond Dam. The dam is not merely a structure and easement onto State land and private property, it is a vital part of our ecosystem, our town’s history, and our quality of life. There could be an opportunity to partner with representatives from Rhode Island, as the Pond stratals the state line.
 
Here is a summary of the community’s primary concerns and the broader public interests at stake:
Gift to the State- Public Trust obligation
It is important to note that Mr. Lester Shippee generously donated 45 acres at 41 Dam Road to the State of Connecticut for all who enjoy Killingly Pond. 
The State of CT also owns property at 1 Dam Road, 135 Pond road and 194 Pond road which permits Connecticut residents free access to Killingly  Pond via State-owned property. 
The interests of the State will now be compromised by the loss of the Pond, reducing the area’s recreational opportunities, impacting wildlife, and eliminating the public enjoyment Mr. Shippee intended with his gift. This loss compounds the urgency for state action, as Connecticut has a vested interest and moral obligation to preserve the value and purpose of this land held in public trust.

Environmental Concerns
•	Killingly Pond supports numerous species of fish and wildlife, including bald eagles and the common loon, which are protected under the Federal Migratory Bird Treaty.
•	The area also supports a rare species of mistletoe.
•	A breach or prolonged drawdown threatens the pond’s entire ecological balance and regional wildlife habitats.

Health and Quality of Life
•	Potable water and well integrity are concerns for nearby residents relying on the aquifer.
•	The exposed lakebed raises concerns for air quality, including odor and airborne particulates.
•	Many residents are experiencing stress and anxiety as they watch the water recede and property conditions deteriorate.

Economic and Property Impacts
•	The drawdown is already devaluing surrounding properties and impacting local tax assessments.
•	Changes in insurance risk ratings may result in higher premiums.

State Park and Public Access
•	Killingly Pond State Park carries obligations for safe maintenance and accessibility for all Connecticut residents.
•	The pond’s historical and cultural significance includes recognition by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names, and longstanding family and tribal histories tied to the area.

Historic and Cultural Preservation
•	The dam and pond have deep roots in Killingly’s milling history and the Pequot Tribe’s presence.
•	Generations of families have preserved and cherished this pond as part of our shared heritage.

Accountability and Maintenance Questions
•	There is uncertainty over maintenance records since the 2008 breach and whether state or private parties last performed repairs.
•	If Wright agreed to maintain the property back in 2008 and it did not, then it has obviously failed in its representations at that time. 
•	Tree and vegetation growth along the backside of the dam has likely contributed to erosion and structural weakening, underscoring the need for an immediate, engineered solution.

We, the residents of Killingly and surrounding communities, are not seeking blame but instead collaboration and resolution. Our hope is that through your leadership, a bill could be introduced to provide the necessary resources and oversight to refurbish and preserve the Killingly Pond Dam before irreversible damage occurs to this vital ecosystem and State landmark.
For your information, the DEEP Dam Safety Division has scheduled a public meeting with the dam’s owner and interested residents for next Thursday, November 6 in the Killingly Town Hall meeting room at 6:00 pm.  DEEP will be reviewing with the owner compliance measures to shore up the integrity of the dam.  It would be great if you or your representative could join us.
Thank you both for your time and your consideration of this important issue. I would welcome the opportunity to meet or participate in a roundtable to discuss the next steps and community engagement.
With gratitude and determination,
 
Sincerely,
 Amy Righter
134 Dam Road, Killingly CT

Dear Representative Bronko,
Thank you for taking the time to learn more about the Alloantibody Exchange (AAE) at Western. I wanted to share some additional context about this initiative and how it’s improving transfusion safety and efficiency for patients across the country.
My name is Rahim Wright, and I serve as the Lead Medical Laboratory Scientist at Danbury Hospital's Blood Bank. Our health system participates in the Alloantibody Exchange alongside Yale–New Haven, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), the University of Michigan, and several others. We’re now very close to having 100% of Connecticut hospitals online—a milestone that will ensure transfusion history follows patients safely wherever they receive care.
Connecticut may be the third smallest state by land area, but it has one of the highest hospital densities in the country. Many patients receive care at multiple facilities within the same week, and often they can’t recall or communicate their transfusion history. The AAE bridges that gap, creating a secure, statewide safety net for patients who depend on blood transfusion support.
About the Alloantibody Exchange (AAE):
The AAE is a national nonprofit platform that securely connects hospital transfusion services, enabling them to share verified antibody and transfusion history data in seconds—directly within their LIS environment.
Patient Safety: Prevents delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions by flagging evanesced (previously identified but currently undetectable) antibodies early.
Efficiency: Reduces antibody workups by 45–90 minutes and replaces phone/fax workflows that used to take 15–18 minutes with instant, automated data sharing (~5 seconds).
Operational Gains: Minimizes surgery delays, expedites transfusions, and reduces staff overtime.
Platform Highlights:
Data shared: ABO/Rh, RBC antigens, antibody history, transfusion requirements (e.g., irradiation, IgA deficiency), monoclonal antibody therapies (e.g., Darzalex), platelet refractoriness, and transfusion totals. (Enhancements underway to include dates of last 3 transfusions.)
Technical setup: Fully compatible with Cerner, SoftBank, WellSky, and other LIS systems; automatic daily refresh; minimal IT involvement.
Security: SOC 2 Type 2 certified, SSO access, optional read-only participation.
Nonprofit mission: Operates as a 501(c)(3) public charity devoted solely to transfusion safety.
www.alloantibody.org
At Danbury Hospital and Yale, the Exchange has become an essential tool—improving turnaround times for complex antibody workups and ensuring safer transfusions for oncology and sickle cell patients. MSKCC’s recent participation marked another milestone toward national collaboration.
I also presented on this topic at the 2024 ASCP Annual Meeting, where I shared how national data sharing can transform transfusion safety. Tragically, a recent case in Maine—where a patient died after receiving incompatible transfusions due to an unshared antibody record—underscored the importance of this work. That incident prompted all Maine hospitals to join the Exchange, demonstrating the life-saving potential of connected data.
We are now seeking state-level support in Connecticut to ensure every hospital can participate and that every resident benefits from a unified transfusion safety network. This initiative represents a rare opportunity to eliminate a long-standing patient safety risk on a statewide scale.
If your team is interested, I’d be happy to coordinate a brief Microsoft Teams meeting with George, the program’s director, to review participation options and discuss how Connecticut can lead the nation in transfusion safety.
Thank you again for your time and your commitment to advancing healthcare for Connecticut residents.

Dear Representative Zullo,

I am writing to express my deep concern over the expansion of Tweed New Haven Airport.  I am a resident of East Haven.  My husband and I live approximately 2.2 miles from the airport.  Our quality of life has decreased immensely since we moved here three years ago.  We did not expect the amount of air traffic to increase like it has in the past three years.  Nor did we anticipate the noise from these old 737’s.  At times, planes are attempting to land past 10:30 pm and into the early hours of the morning. They leave promptly at 6:30 am six days a week.  We can’t speak to one another when we’re sitting outside on our patio when a plane is flying overhead because of the loudness of the aircraft.  Nor can we speak on a cell phone outside when a plane is flying overhead.  When our home windows are open during the nicer weather, we are unable to speak on our phones inside or hear the television when a plane is flying overhead.  And our cell phone calls are frequently dropped as planes are flying overhead.

I expect you know what I'm talking about when I say when I'm in my backyard garden I feel like I can touch an airplane?  Do you know what it’s like to be out for a walk and a plane is directly overhead?  I would also believe that you have sat on Stoddard, Maturo, South End Roads in East Haven and watched these planes come into the area to land.  It's unnerving how low and close to the homes and streets they are.   Have you watched a plane attempt to land in the fog at Tweed?  I have.  It’s scary.  Sometimes at the last minute the pilot decides he can’t land on the runway due to heavy fog and rapidly pulls the plane up to abort landing and fly elsewhere.  Or they circle around and try again.

Add the airport traffic and people will be looking for ways around Hemingway and Coe.  I expect the alternate routes of South End and Silver Sands to see an increase in volume. Sincerely,

Donna Moore

I am contacting you as a representative of the Hebron Historical Society. We are seeking your help and support to have a State historic marker(sign) installed in the Amston section of Hebron.
  
The marker is to commemorate a Revolutionary War encampment of Duke de Lauzun’s French Legion in the Amston section of Hebron. The men spent one night in Hebron before resuming their march east, along now Rt66 toward New York.

The original group of Lauzon’s Legion, 600 strong, split into two groups at the intersection of now Rt207 &16 in Exeter after departing Lebanon on June 21,1781.
 The 300 men who took the North-Westerly Rd.(Rt207) spent the night of June 21, 1781 encamped near the current intersection of Rt207 & 85 in Amston. 

Hebron Historical Society member, Frank Kunz, has identified the approximate location based on research by Robert A. Selig, PH.D.. 
The marker would need to be placed on State property.                    

Dr. Selig completed a survey for the State of Ct in 1999 titled Rochambeau in Ct; Tracing his Journey, Historic and Architectural Survey Ct Historical Society Commission. 
Dr. Selig is the National Park Service consultant for the Washington - Rochambeau Route (W3R-US)
.  
We hope you will support us in our effort to pay tribute to the French Legion who gave up their lives, who fought for our freedom and to keep the memory of the Franco-American alliance alive.

Sincerely,
Susan Porter
